name: Finding Our Place on Earth and in the Sky
description: Stars, compasses, chronometers and satellites: how sailors learned where they were at sea, and how astronomers learned where the Earth sits among the planets and galaxies.

checkpoints.name: Stars and sails
checkpoints.note: Greek and Islamic scholars built astrolabes and geared machines like the Antikythera mechanism to model the sky. Polynesian navigators crossed the open Pacific by reading stars, swells and birds, and northern sailors steered by Polaris.

checkpoints.name: Compass and chart
checkpoints.note: The compass came from China and portolan charts guided Mediterranean pilots. Zheng He's treasure fleets crossed the Indian Ocean, sailors measured star heights with the Jacob's staff, Prince Henry the Navigator sent Portuguese captains down Africa's coast, Magellan's expedition sailed round the world, and Copernicus put the Sun at the centre.

checkpoints.name: The longitude problem
checkpoints.note: The telescope let Galileo find the moons of Jupiter, and Kepler's laws described the planets' orbits. After disasters at sea, the sextant and John Harrison's marine chronometer let navigators find longitude, and Cook's first voyage observed the transit of Venus to measure the solar system.

checkpoints.name: Radio and the galaxies
checkpoints.note: Henrietta Leavitt found a way to measure the distance of far stars, and Edwin Hubble showed that the Milky Way is one galaxy among many. Gyrocompasses gave ships a north free of magnetism, and radar and LORAN used radio waves to find ships and aircraft through night and fog.

checkpoints.name: The satellite age
checkpoints.note: Tracking the radio signal of Sputnik 1 in 1957 showed that satellites could be used to fix a position on Earth, and the Global Positioning System turned that idea into a map in every pocket.
